title: Explaining a Game Concept: Goals, Actions and Conditions Beyond Comparisons

scenes.title: What this video will help you explain
lines: When describing a game that does not exist yet, can a familiar title make everyone picture the same thing?
We will put Pepper Grinder’s movement into verbs, then distinguish conditions through The Plucky Squire’s actions across illustrated surfaces and a desk.
By the end, you can write the goal, actions and conditions in three sentences and use a listener’s questions to find what is missing.
Let us begin by watching the character drill out of yellow terrain.

scenes.title: Actual action: drilling out toward another space
lines: The character changes direction inside yellow terrain, emerges, and moves through the air. Notice the brambles between routes and the separated pieces of terrain.
Hanging from a hook and launching from a cannon are different kinds of movement. Calling all of it running can hide what the character actually does.
In the dark cave, the character curves along a low passage and emerges into the air again. Start by writing the action verbs and the spaces where those actions happen.
Here we are describing visible movement. This short demonstration does not establish the exact buttons or the rules for every kind of terrain.

scenes.title: One title can suggest different scenes
lines: If a new concept is introduced only as being like a familiar game, listeners fill in the gaps with the parts they remember.
Imagine two hypothetical listeners. One might picture movement over obstacles, while the other first pictures fighting enemies.
This is an explanation exercise, not a result from a user study. We are avoiding the assumption that hearing the same title means picturing the same actions.
If you use a comparison, say which part you mean. That helps prevent the listener from supplying the rest of your unbuilt game’s rules.

scenes.title: Actual action: moving across pictures and a desk
lines: Now watch The Plucky Squire. Begin with walking on an illustrated book surface and crossing a gap between books.
Passing through a green entry point brings the character onto the three-dimensional desk. Another shot shows movement between the desk and a pictured surface with printed doors.
There is also a sequence of approaching an entry point on a cup and entering its printed surface. Separately, watch the character leave that surface and appear on the desk.
Saying only that the game mixes two and three dimensions leaves out where the character enters and what happens there. Describe the surface and the entry point together.
This is a desk inside the game, rather than a live-action advertisement outside it. The explanation is based on actions visibly performed in that virtual space.

scenes.title: Where, what action, and what visible change
lines: When writing the explanation, connect the space, the action verb and the visible change: approaching an entry point on the desk and entering a printed surface, for example.
Adding this sentence next to a phrase like enjoyable movement gives the listener a more concrete action to picture.
A title or genre can provide context. Use your own sentence to convey the central action of the new concept.

scenes.title: Actual action: movement has conditions
lines: Return to Pepper’s waterside and routes above lava. A walkable bridge, curved terrain and an elastic purple surface show different spaces and movements.
Specifying where the movement happens, such as a sloping route or an ice surface beside wooden braces, narrows what your explanation covers.
During Plucky’s rocket movement, the character rises among spool tops and card ledges, strikes enemies, and approaches an entry point on a wall.
Also watch the character descend into a mug, pass a glowing object, and rise again. You can describe ascent, descent and the spaces reached separately.
These observations do not establish unlimited flight or a fuel-refill rule. Keep visible conditions separate from questions that need further checking.

scenes.title: Separate observations from decisions to make
lines: For a new concept, decide how entry points will be indicated and when an action can be performed again.
Write these questions beside the observed facts, in a separate place. A time limit or a cost is a design question we are proposing here.
Filling a gap with a remembered assumption about a reference game can make an undecided rule sound settled.
Explain the conditions you have established, and leave undecided ones as questions. That also shows the listener where their input is needed.

scenes.title: Actual action: character movement and book tilt
lines: In the mine sequence, the character approaches an entry point on the illustrated surface and emerges onto the desk. Distinguish the character walking from the book itself tilting.

When the book tilts left, the yellow key moves left; in another portion, it moves right. Record the visible directions, but this demonstration does not establish the exact input or a rule for every object.
For your new concept, spell out what moves and what changes. That sentence exposes conditions you may have expected a familiar title to supply.

scenes.title: Actual action: distinguish movement, entry and combat
lines: On the desk, the character approaches and attacks enemies and throws an object. Describing movement through the space is not the same as describing how enemies are confronted.
Inside the blue printed surface, the character jumps and strikes enemies. The surface on which the action takes place has changed from the desk.
Approaching an entry point on a large cylinder and entering its picture is another action. Distinguish entry from combat that follows it.
Adding a sentence for what happens in each space reveals differences hidden by the phrase changing dimensions.

scenes.title: Three sentences: goal, action and conditions, connection
lines: Now write a new concept in three sentences. The first gives the player’s goal; the second gives the repeated action and its central conditions.
The third explains how that action connects to another. The following is our explanation exercise using the scenes we have watched.
The goal is to reach the next platform. The action is drilling along a route inside soft terrain. Emerging from that terrain connects the action to moving through the air toward another space.

These sentences do not reproduce the developer’s design document or establish the game’s overall goal. For your own concept, decide the goal and permitted conditions and write them in the same structure.

scenes.title: Actual action: do not invent rules across edits
lines: A pictured surface where a word and lighting change, matching colored balls, and combat are different actions. Do not automatically treat the next edited shot as the result of the previous action.
Pepper’s water vehicle also appears in separate shots: traveling over flat water and rising over waves. This edit alone does not establish one continuous chase.
Shooting on the cylinder’s picture includes ground movement and airborne attacks in separate sections. Here we observe each movement and the approaching targets.
Some footage comes from an official presentation of assistance features. We do not turn that presentation into a claim about default difficulty or how every entry point is shown.
As you read the sentences for your new concept, separate what the footage establishes from what you will decide. Do not let the reference make those promises for you.

scenes.title: Use restatement to find what is missing
lines: Ask the listener to describe, in their own words, what they would do first. The question checks the action you conveyed rather than asking them to identify a reference title.
If a hypothetical answer is entering any wall, check whether the condition about entry points was missing. Restatement is a checking method we are proposing.
Check whether the goal and actions were understood as intended, identify undecided conditions, and clarify the necessary sentences. The listener’s questions show where the concept needs more detail.

scenes.title: Actual action: separate entry, combat and visible results
lines: On the illustrated surface, the character strikes enemies and moves along the route. Do not bundle entry movement and the combat after entry into one action.
A later red chest opens and a card graphic appears. The earlier movement of the key does not justify promising that every chest opens or that combat ends.
Check whether a listener can separate these differences in their own words. Distinguishing the visible result from a connection condition still to be decided reveals missing questions.

scenes.title: Add the setting and target through observed actions
lines: On the illustrated page, the character approaches enemies, fights and moves to another platform. Separating the bright path from the dark one also brings out the setting hidden by the single word fight.

On the desk, the character walks along a route or attacks near objects. Treat the exit from the illustrated page and the movement on the desk as separate shots, and you can describe where each action happens.
Pepper’s movement out near water and above lava is different from firing toward an enemy. Describe the movement and its target together.
In the mine, the character moves to avoid an approaching enemy and attacks. These actions do not establish every condition of combat.

scenes.title: A final check against visible actions
lines: Read these last scenes as action verbs too. On pictured surfaces, the character fights and climbs stairs; on the desk, the character follows a route or rises with a rocket.
Pepper launches from cannons and enters a large device. In other shots, the device moves and fires. These scenes do not establish the entry cost or a victory condition.
When the action changes, reconsider the goal and conditions you need to explain. Recalling one familiar title does not by itself communicate these differences.
Write your own new concept as three sentences: the goal, the action and its conditions, and the connection to another action. Even if you add a comparison, explain the central actions directly.
Then use the listener’s restatement to find missing conditions. Check whether the same actions were understood, beyond whether both people know the same title.
